intro.es: A clinic reports that waiting has almost disappeared. A volunteer follows the people who no longer appear in its figures.
intro.en: A clinic reports that waiting has almost disappeared. A volunteer follows the people who no longer appear in its figures.

mission.es: Examine where the institution draws the boundary of its queue, and whose experience that boundary excludes.
mission.en: Examine where the institution draws the boundary of its queue, and whose experience that boundary excludes.

content.targetText:
At the clinic where I volunteered, the old waiting room had been reduced to a corridor with six chairs. The rest of the space was now a consultation suite, its glass wall displaying a graph of what the director called recovered time. Patients received a number on their phones and were told to arrive only when it turned green. A poster beside the entrance promised that nobody would have to sit for hours beneath fluorescent lights again. It was a persuasive promise. I remembered the previous room: damp coats, a television with no sound, and the small humiliations of asking whether a number had been missed. I did not wish it back. Yet the first morning the new system opened, I found a dozen people standing under the awning across the street. Their phones were dark; their appointments, according to the graph, had not begun. Rain made the pavement shine like a second, less comfortable waiting room. A woman said she had come early because the bus from her village came only twice a day. She was neither late nor, by the clinic's definition, waiting.

The director's ledger counted the interval between a green notification and a consultation. By that measure the average wait had fallen sharply. The figure was accurate within its chosen jurisdiction, and the staff were justified in celebrating one real improvement: no one now sat inside wondering whether a paper ticket had been lost. But the number also conferred a kind of invisibility. Travel, uncertainty and the effort of remaining close enough to answer a summons had moved beyond the ledger's edge. The director called this freedom: patients could spend that time wherever they wished. In principle, they could. In practice, a person who left the neighbourhood risked missing the alert, while someone without mobile data had to borrow certainty from a stranger. The system had not abolished the queue. It had made the queue conditional, scattered and harder to see. I wrote that sentence in my notebook, then crossed out “made” and wrote “allowed.” The distinction mattered to me. A software change could not be held responsible for the bus timetable; neither could a clinic claim a victory over waiting while refusing to ask what its timetable demanded of people.

Miriam, the porter, kept a private list of the people sheltering outside. She did not call it a second queue, because she feared the word might become a reason for management to move them on. Instead, she noted practical things: a man who could not hear his phone above the traffic; a woman whose battery had failed; a teenager translating the notifications for his grandfather. Miriam's care was quiet, but it carried an awkward cost. Her list preserved people who would otherwise vanish from the official account, while also making their access depend on one employee's unpaid attention. The director praised her initiative at a staff meeting, an ostensible compliment that left the policy untouched. When I suggested that the clinic provide a sheltered place to wait without requiring a green number, he asked whether I wanted to restore the crowded room we had worked so hard to empty. His question was not cynical. Space really was scarce, and extra chairs would displace a consultation desk. But it offered only two pictures of care: the old room or the new graph. The wet pavement, where the decision's consequences had settled, appeared in neither.

At the next committee meeting I proposed a different measurement. The clinic could ask patients when they first had to organise their day around the appointment, and record the time they spent within reach of a possible alert. The director objected that such an interval could not be attributed to the clinic alone. He was right. It would include buses, employers, relatives, batteries and the ordinary disorder of a life. I said that this was precisely why we should record it, though I knew the answer sounded too neat. A number broad enough to include every inconvenience might cease to guide any particular decision. A number narrow enough to guide a decision might conceal the people affected by it. The committee agreed to trial an optional question at check-in, but it declined to change the published graph. The graph remained useful for scheduling rooms; it was merely being asked to stand for a larger truth than it could bear. We had not resolved how to measure that truth, and I was uneasy with my own readiness to put other people's uncertainty into another spreadsheet.

Weeks later the awning was empty when I arrived. The director pointed to it as evidence that the new arrangement had finally worked. Miriam said the people from the village had learned to wait in the supermarket cafe, where they bought the cheapest tea and watched their screens. I went there once. The tables offered warmth and a socket, but their welcome was provisional: a cup purchased at nine did not guarantee a place at noon. One of the patients asked whether I had come to take a survey. I said no, although I had brought a notebook. I closed it. His question made me aware that observation, too, could turn a person's afternoon into evidence for somebody else's argument. The clinic had improved the part of waiting it could see, and that improvement deserved its name. The hours outside its frame had not disappeared. Whether they belonged to the clinic's responsibility was still contested; whether they belonged to the patients' day was not. When my own phone finally lit green, I found that I had been waiting for an answer the graph could never provide.
